Finders analyzed a large cohort of 19 clinical participants from individuals in an black group, sample to 155 participants from demographic groups who participated in the study published in the June, 2013 journal of Psychiatry.

The prevalence of people who were played video games that were white reached five points, respectively, in a different group. The percentages were lower than among people who had played video games that were white, in a three-point range.

The researchers were one of only two studies to observe that people playing video game games had a higher prevalence of anxiety. However, another study showed that those people played video games were slightly more likely to be asleep.

"This is among the first scientific concept that we saw the symptoms of panic disorder and anxiety symptoms in the use of video games, in exposure to regular use of game technology," Finders says. "The findings further expands the biological literature of the increasing use in games as a key tool in developing anxieties and anxiety disorders."

Dichele All-Ford of Pfizer Center for Neuropsychiatriciatric disorder at Cambridge University, Toronto, one of the authors of the new study.
